Act as the implementation sub-agent for this task.

Implement in /home/diogenes/Projects/twyne. User asked to make Sentence Bench actually useful and requested frontier research by Astra max, Fable 5.1 and Opus high, then another Opus medium implementation. Their independent and cross-critique rounds converged on the scope below. You own Sentence Bench component/CSS, related contract/helper/tests/docs and ONLY necessary sentence-lab branches of tracker/in-flow tools/selection integration. You are not alone in shared checkout: inspect status, preserve unrelated dirty work, don't revert others. Another Opus medium owns persona feedback cards and expanded comments; do NOT touch those files, comment-mark.ts or shared comment infrastructure. No commit/deploy. All shell commands prefix rtk including chain segments. Read applicable AGENTS.md; use Impeccable skill /home/diogenes/.agents/skills/impeccable/SKILL.md (context script setup and product reference), and plan-execution-graph /home/diogenes/.codex/skills/plan-execution-graph/SKILL.md for own dependency planning; no further agents. Avoid Convex changes.
DECIDED DIRECTION: 'Compare a revision' (or equally clear label): explicitly select one source sentence; preserve anchored original, one writer-editable trial, visible paragraph context by default, word diff and original/trial preview. No history required. Optional explicit 'Read the difference' via EXISTING configured prose transport: zero to two grounded interpretations of consequential changes in meaning, no generated rewrites, quality/safety scores or preferred-version ranking. Each observation references verbatim original/trial phrases and any context used; validate references in code, bind result to exact original/trial/context, invalidate on edits, discard stale requests, cancellation/provider failure preserves copyable trial. Empty result says no observations returned, NEVER claims unchanged meaning/safety. No Jev/tiny model semantic fallback. Respect existing wallet/provider auth/metering, do not bypass. Keep model request explicit, no automatic paid requests.
Use revision applies one undoable edit and returns editor focus. Keep original/Escape closes without mutation. Grammar is advisory for writer-authored trial, permit nonempty fragments/multiple replacement sentences within size limit. Source integrity/stale checks remain enforcement. Exact selection targeting among duplicate sentences; refuse unsupported selection clearly, never silently pick longest/narrow multi-sentence input. Preserve supported inline marks/citations; explicit refusal if replacement cannot safely preserve unsupported structure. Don't flatten silently.
Replace tabs/candidate picker in this surface: remove regex/generated rewrite lists, Words/Place/Compare panels, meaning probabilities, repeated caveats, automatic rewrite/move pop-open paths. Don't delete shared helper code or global behaviours blindly; inspect references and update relevant existing tests/docs/fixtures/walkthroughs honestly. Keep existing editor invitation and read-aloud access if low overhead; no new Park, persistence, version stack, A/B narration or heuristic semantic-risk panel. This is a focused hypothesis, not validated demand; report that limit.
Validation: focused unit/integration tests of observation parser/binding/stale cases and editor targeting/apply; real browser narrow width/long content, cold-start open, edit/diff/read flow (mock okay only clearly labelled), close/focus, source stale handling, one Undo. T3 preview preferred: preview_status then preview_open. Run relevant lint/typecheck/build tests, distinguishing baseline failures. If authenticated live provider unavailable, don't claim actual semantic quality. Don't let external setup stall local implementation; report precise limits.
Deliver changed files, implementation summary, checks/browser evidence, running server URL, any remaining substantive risk. FULL CROSS-CRITIQUE FINDINGS:
ASTRA ROUND TWO:
I recommend **“Compare a revision”**: select one sentence, write one alternative, request a short contextual reading of the difference, then apply or discard. It must work with **zero ledger history**.

I am narrowing my first-round recommendation. A scratch field, contextual preview and diff are useful mechanics, but they do not establish a product advantage over ordinary editing. The proposed advantage is helping the writer notice a consequential interpretation they had not considered. That remains an unvalidated hypothesis.

**Fable’s strongest argument is that alternatives arrive before diagnosis.** I agree. But identifying where edits accumulate does not explain why the sentence is troublesome. Unchanged words need not be settled; repeatedly changing an ending may reflect a problem elsewhere. Calling a common-prefix calculation a “diagnosis” overstates it. Likewise, a Jev sentence-job label and probability cannot establish the writer’s intention. Such interpretations require task-specific evaluation.

The ledger also filters meaning-bearing changes: an existing test deliberately treats **“carries” → “carried”** as one attempt. It is useful editing history, not a reliable record of semantic decisions. [Ledger test](/home/diogenes/Projects/twyne/src/utils/sentence-ledger.test.ts:45)

**Opus’s strongest argument is that preserving the writer’s alternatives, especially through Park, protects ownership and momentum.** I accept that and withdraw any suggestion that finishing the sentence should be the only successful outcome. However, Park addresses a different job: retaining unresolved work across sessions. Durable anchoring, storage and annotation behaviour make it substantial, particularly alongside the concurrent comment work. It cannot rescue a history-first cold start.

Adjacent comparison deserves testing: ABScribe reported benefits in a 12-writer study of AI-assisted variation workflows. That does not validate a ledger-based Twyne bench. Research on ownership also supports caution about intervention, rather than proving writers want this particular interface. [ABScribe](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.00117), [Co-Writing with AI, on Human Terms](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.12488)

The concrete cold start would be:

1. A writer opens a manuscript after a reload. There is no sentence history. They select the middle sentence below and choose **Compare a revision**.

   > Mara learned about the sale that morning. **She had not told her brother that the house was sold.** He was already packing for his visit.

2. The paragraph appears immediately, with the selected sentence copied into one editable trial. The writer types:

   > She had kept the sale from her brother.

3. They choose **Read the difference**. An acceptable authored example of the response is:

   > **“had not told” → “had kept the sale from”**  
   > The trial can suggest deliberate concealment. The original leaves her reason for not telling him open.

4. They decide whether secrecy is intended, revise again, use the trial, or discard it. Application is one undoable edit; focus returns to the passage.

This is a proposed interaction, not an observed successful session. Some writers will find that observation obvious. **For them, this example supplies no reason to open the tool.**

The potential value is an alternative reading of the writer’s own revision. Undo already supplies reversibility. A description such as “you shortened the ending” fails the added-value test.

I would retain the anchored original, one trial, visible paragraph context, literal differences, stale-source protection and one-step Undo. Remove the four-tab structure, rule/generated rewrite lists, sentence-job rankings, meaning probabilities and automatic sentence offers. Remove the single-word Alternatives entry from this feature; keep the existing selection read-aloud action. Do not add a version stack, contested-span summary, Park, deletion workflow or A/B narration.

The reading should return **zero to two material observations**, each attached to exact original/trial quotations and any context it uses. Display these as interpretations, without a preferred-version ranking or safety verdict. An empty result means no observation was returned, not that meaning was preserved. Grammar remains advisory. The writer may deliberately change meaning or use a fragment.

For implementation, I would set these boundaries:

- Own `sentence-bench.tsx/.css`, its catalog contract, and only the Sentence Lab branches of `in-flow-tools.ts` and `struggle-tracker.ts`. Add a small typed comparison request/parser helper using the existing configured prose transport. No Jev or tiny-model semantic fallback.
- Accept one explicitly anchored source sentence and a nonempty replacement within the existing size limit. Permit replacement by multiple sentences. Reject unsupported selections clearly; never silently choose the longest sentence. The current manual controller contains fallback matching that needs tightening. [Controller](/home/diogenes/Projects/twyne/src/components/editor/extensions/struggle-tracker.ts:1412)
- Bind each response to the exact original, trial and supplied context. Editing any input invalidates its reading. Reject malformed or unmatched evidence references. Quote matching proves provenance only.
- Preserve the trial on request failure or source invalidation. Make it copyable when application is unavailable. Preserve inline formatting and citations where supported; refuse unsupported replacements explicitly rather than silently flattening them.
- Coordinate any necessary selection-callback change in the already-dirty `twyne-editor.tsx`. Persona cards, expanded comments, `comment-mark.ts`, shared comment infrastructure, Convex and ledger persistence are outside scope.

Update fixtures, affected instrument tests, manual descriptions and walkthroughs to describe the reduced feature honestly.

Acceptance requires separate evidence:

- **Interaction correctness:** fresh-session opening without history; no generation or manuscript mutation on open; exact targeting among duplicate sentences; no silent multi-sentence narrowing; valid fragments; intentional meaning changes; stale source/context/trial responses; cancellation and provider failure; one-step Undo and restored focus. Exercise keyboard use, long text and a narrow viewport in the real browser.
- **Model behaviour:** evaluate the actual configured model on negation, uncertainty, quantities, agency, timing, literary ambiguity and qualifications preserved elsewhere in context. Include unchanged meaning and intentional changes. Record false alarms and misses separately. Mocked responses establish application behaviour, not reading quality.
- **Product value:** compare real revision tasks using editing plus Undo, local comparison alone, comparison with readings, and the existing editor invitation. Look for useful decisions and voluntary reuse without increasing unwanted changes or decision time. More opens or more accepted edits do not establish success.

Two objections remain decisive. First, this helps someone who already has an alternative; it does not solve “I dislike this sentence and have no idea what to write.” Its entry label must respect that limitation. Second, the existing editor invitation already carries source and unapplied proposal. If that path provides equally useful readings with less effort, the separate bench should be retired. [Existing handoff](/home/diogenes/Projects/twyne/src/utils/instrument-room.ts:328)

Model misreadings, limited context and provider latency remain costs. Evidence anchors and restrained wording cannot eliminate them. A local-only comparison may remain usable offline, but I would not present it as the answer to the user’s objection.

This was a read-only source and research review using Impeccable guidance. No files changed; no tests or live browser validation were run.



FABLE ROUND TWO:
**Fable, round 2.** Read only. I checked the facts the objection rests on: the ledger is in memory only (no reference in idb or convex-sync), a wording settles only after a complete sentence, 5 s or cursor exit, and a Harper spelling pass, and manual Rework resolves to one sentence by cursor or text match with no ledger requirement. Apply still vetoes on any new Harper issue, even for the writer's own copy.

## Where I was wrong

**My round-1 design depends on history that usually does not exist.** The contested-span diagnosis needs two or more settled wordings. Opus's point that history dies on reload, plus my own settle-threshold caveat, means the common open is manual Rework on a sentence with zero or one wording. A design whose best case needs four settled versions and whose common case degrades to "here is your sentence" is not a minimum useful workflow. I withdraw it as the core.

**Opus's "same / still changing" line is the same idea with the same weakness**, and Opus's own section 8 says so: when the writer restructures, it has nothing to say, and when they only swap a verb, it states what they already know. Both of us built the first screen on a thin data source.

**Astra's design works cold.** It needs only the sentence, its paragraph, and whatever the writer types next. That is the decisive advantage, and I now think it is the right spine.

## Where Astra's argument is weakest, and how to answer it

Astra's own strongest objection: ordinary editing plus Undo may already cover trial editing. I think it does, for the trial itself. A textarea copy of the sentence is not a feature. What the editor cannot do is show the writer what their edit *did to the claim*. So the bench earns its place only if the semantic observation is real, and Astra's step 4 is the entire product. Two risks follow.

1. **Obvious observations.** "You removed 'may'" is a diff, not an observation. The model must be constrained to the *consequence* for the reader: what became definite, who now acts, what quantity or time shifted, what qualification elsewhere in the paragraph the edit now contradicts. If the model cannot name a consequence, it must return nothing, and the UI must show "No change in what this claims" rather than padding.
2. **Wrong observations.** A frontier prose model, not Jev or a fill-mask pack, does this read. Evidence spans are validated against code-owned text, and a validated span proves only that the quote exists. The writer can dismiss an observation in one click; dismissal is recorded for the eval corpus, never argued with.

Against Opus's Park: I like it, but it writes machine-made alternatives into the comment layer that another agent is redesigning right now, and it mostly matters when there are versions to park. Defer it.

## One workflow: Try a revision, then see what it changed

**Trigger.** Select a sentence, choose **Rework** (relabel **Try a revision**). Remove the three-wordings auto-open and the three-moves Place open. The struggle signal can keep its quiet margin tick; it opens the same surface.

**Cold start, realistic sentence.** Morgan has:

> Most of what Hallam left behind was paperwork, though the letter suggested he had meant to come back.

They select it, choose Try a revision. The bench shows the paragraph with this sentence editable in place, original wording held beneath it, one neighbour each side visible by default. No candidates, no tabs. Morgan types:

> Hallam left mostly paperwork, and the letter proved he had meant to come back.

Word diff appears as they type. They press **Check what changed**. One observation returns:

> **"suggested" → "proved"** The trial states as fact what the original left as the letter's implication. The next sentence ("Nobody knows whether the letter reached her") still treats his intention as uncertain.

Morgan changes "proved" back to "suggested", keeps the tighter opening, reads the paragraph, presses **Use revision**. One undo step, cursor at the end of the sentence, bench closes.

If Morgan had wanted "proved", **Use revision** still works. The observation advised; nothing vetoed.

**What makes it worth opening.** A sentence of consequences for the reader that the writer did not get from the diff and could not get from Undo. If that line is usually obvious or absent, the bench should be retired. That is the research question, stated up front.

**Removed.** Rewrite candidate list, regex rule rewrites, model wording generation, Words tab and bundled thesaurus, Place tab, Compare panel, About disclosures and per-row caveats, Jev meaning probability, Harper as a veto on writer-authored prose (demote to an inline notice on the trial). Single-word Alternatives is cut from this surface; whether it gets a popover is a separate decision.

**Retained.** Selection anchor and sentence range, stale-source check, ghost preview of the trial in place, word diff, Hear (trial between neighbours), one-undo apply, Ask an editor link, Context visible by default.

## Acceptance criteria

- Opens on any single sentence with no ledger history and is fully usable offline except the check, which is labelled unavailable rather than hidden.
- Check returns zero to two observations. Each cites an original phrase and a trial phrase that exist verbatim in the respective texts, or it is discarded.
- No observation is a restatement of the diff. Eval corpus includes trials where the only honest answer is "no change in what this claims", and the model must return empty on those.
- Use revision applies in one undo step; a changed source blocks apply and keeps the trial.
- Harper problems in the trial show as a notice; apply is not blocked by them.
- Keyboard: Escape closes, Enter in the check button runs, focus returns to the editor at the revised span.

## Implementation boundaries and tests

- **`src/components/in-flow/sentence-bench.tsx`**: replace the tab body with trial field, diff, Check, Use, Keep. Do not touch `comment-mark.ts` or persona card files.
- **`src/utils/in-flow-tools.ts`**: new prompt taking original, trial, paragraph, goal and audience; returns JSON observations with `originalSpan`, `trialSpan`, `consequence`. Validate spans in code. Unit test: valid, invalid span, empty.
- **`struggle-tracker.ts`**: `applyVariant` stops failing on lint issues (keeps `completeSentence` and stale checks); remove auto-open paths for rewrite count and moves. Update existing tests that assert auto-open.
- **`selection-actions.tsx`**: relabel; multi-sentence selection narrows as today but names the chosen sentence.
- Docs: manual, narration script and `manual-films.ts` describe the old tabs. Screenshot and narration regeneration is a real cost; list it, do not skip it.
- **Measure before phase 2**: log opens, checks run, observations dismissed, Use versus Keep, and reopen within ten minutes.

## Unresolved objections, not to be papered over

- **The whole value is one model call.** If observations are usually obvious, the correct outcome is deleting the bench, not adding tabs back. Nobody in this round has evidence either way; the user's own week of use is the only test.
- **This helps evaluate an edit, not find one.** A writer with no trial in mind gets nothing. Generation was removed deliberately for ownership; some writers will miss it.
- **Hallucinated consequences.** Validated quotes do not validate interpretation. The UI must never say "verified".
- **Thin history is now ignored, not used.** When a ledger does hold several settled wordings, Opus's and my version stack would be genuinely useful. It belongs as phase 2, gated on logged evidence that histories reach two or more wordings in practice.
- **Deleting shipped, documented behaviour** (Words, Place, rule rewrites). If the parent wants continuity, park them behind the selection menu rather than delete.

OPUS ROUND TWO:
I'm Opus, round 2. I made no edits and spawned no agents.

## What I checked in the code this round

- **Manual opens have no history.** The sentence ledger starts empty on every load (`struggle-tracker.ts:233`). Its first settle records the current text as the only wording (`sentence-ledger.ts:231–260`). The only persisted history, `draft-trajectory.ts`, keeps paragraph excerpts cut to 180 characters. So when a writer opens the bench by hand, a sentence they haven't rewritten this session has exactly one wording.
- **This weakens Fable's design and my own round-1 design on the main deliberate entry point.** Fable's contested span and my version stack both have nothing to show there.
- **Of the three proposals, only Astra's works from a cold start.**

## Responding to the strongest arguments

**Astra: "Did I change what I meant?"** I adopt this as the frame. One thing needs correcting: Astra's proposal still depends on a model reading for its value, and that is where the "semantic inspection can be wrong" objection hits hardest. My revision is to split it in two:
- **A code layer that runs automatically.** It reports only what can be observed: words from risk categories that are in the original but missing from the trial. The categories are hedges and modals, negation, numbers and quantifiers, named or capitalised terms, and deleted runs of four or more words.
- **A model reading that only adds to it.** It interprets what the code found, and the code layer never depends on it.

**Fable: diagnose, don't propose.** I agree. But the diagnosis that pure code can make reliably is "what you removed", not "what this sentence is for". Fable's Jev job label is a small model acting as semantic authority with no validation. The brief rules that out, so I drop it.

Fable also argues that the contested span names the decision the writer is circling. I concede that it mostly tells the writer what they did a few minutes ago. My "same / still changing" line has the same weakness. Both are demoted.

**My own round 1: Park.** It is the best idea I had, but it depends on `comment-mark.ts`, which the persona-card work is changing right now. It is deferred, not dropped.

**"Ordinary editing plus Undo already covers trial editing."** This is partly true. The bench's real advantage is narrower: **the original stays visible and intact while you change the trial.** In the editor, getting back to the original means undoing, and that throws away the trial. That is the whole case for opening the surface. If writers don't need the two versions side by side, the bench should go.

## The one workflow: "Keep the original while you try"

**Entry**
- The selection toolbar shows **Try a revision** for a selection within one paragraph.
- The original is the exact selected range. Today's silent narrowing to one sentence is removed.
- Single-word selections no longer show **Alternatives**.
- The automatic struggle trigger can still open the bench. When it does, the earlier settled wordings from the ledger appear as chips that load into the trial. This is the only use of history, and an empty ledger just means no chips.

**Surface**
- The paragraph is always shown, with the selection in place. An **Original / Trial** toggle swaps the selection in the paragraph using the existing ghost preview.
- One editable trial, pre-filled with the original.
- A **Gone from the original** line, from the code layer. It updates as the writer types and needs no click and no network.
- Optionally, a model reading. It is requested with **Read the change**, or runs automatically once per distinct pair when the code layer flags a loss. It returns at most two observations. Each quotes the exact original and trial phrases, and an observation is dropped if its quotes don't match the text exactly. It never gives a score, a "safe" badge, or a rewrite. It only uses the writer's configured prose provider, never Jev or an on-device model.

**Decision**
- **Use revision**: one undoable transaction. Grammar findings are advice only and don't block it.
- **Keep original** (Esc).
- If the source changed while the bench was open, applying is blocked and the trial is kept for recovery.

**Cold start, realistic sentence**

> Most of the residents we interviewed said they would probably move if rents rose again, though few had looked at other neighbourhoods.

The writer selects it, chooses **Try a revision**, and tightens the trial to:

> Most residents said they would move if rents rose again.

Without any network, the bench shows:

> **Gone from the original:** "we interviewed" · "probably" · "though few had looked at other neighbourhoods"

If a provider is configured, the model reading adds:

> "would probably move" → "would move": the residents' intention now reads as firm. The dropped clause was the paragraph's evidence that the threat may be idle.

The writer can respond in three ways:
- Restore "probably" and use the revision.
- Keep the cut on purpose.
- Keep the original.

In each case they can still see the original while deciding.

**What makes it worth opening:** you can cut hard without losing the original, and you get a list of the qualifiers you dropped. Neither depends on the bench having seen any earlier versions.

## Removed and kept

**Removed**
- Model-generated rewrites and the generic rewrite prompt (`in-flow-tools.ts:320`).
- The regex wordiness rules, intensifier removal, semicolon split and clause fronting.
- The Words tab and thesaurus.
- The Place tab and the automatic opening after three moves.
- The Compare panel.
- The About disclosures and per-row caveats.
- The Jev meaning probability (`struggle-tracker.ts:959`).
- The grammar veto on writer-authored text.

**Kept**
- Anchoring to the selected range, ghost preview, stale checks, one-undo apply.
- **Hear**, as a single "hear trial in context" button.
- The existing Ask an editor link, left exactly as it is.

## Implementation boundaries

**Change**
- `src/utils/sentence-bench.ts`: add a pure function `changeLosses(original, trial)`, built on `sentenceWordDiff`, and delete the candidate generators.
- `src/components/in-flow/sentence-bench.tsx`: replace the tabbed body.
- `struggle-tracker.ts`:
  - pass the exact selection range;
  - remove the candidate pipeline, the meaning check and the move-triggered opening;
  - make grammar advisory on apply.
- `in-flow-tools.ts`: replace the rewrite prompt with a reading prompt that returns `{originalQuote, trialQuote, consequence}[]`, capped at two.
- `selection-actions.tsx`: change the label and hide the action for single words.
- Manual text, narration and films that describe the tabs (`manual-films.ts`): flag them for the parent. The screenshot and narration pipeline is a separate step.

**Do not touch**
- `comment-mark.ts`, the persona panels, `personas-panel.tsx`.
- Room or editor-feedback rendering.
- `flow-surface.tsx`, beyond the bench mount if that is strictly needed. It is modified in the working tree, so coordinate first.

**Tests**
- **`changeLosses` unit tests:**
  - flags a removed hedge, negation, number, quantifier and proper term;
  - flags a deleted run of four or more words;
  - flags nothing for a pure reorder;
  - flags nothing for additions only;
  - flags nothing for an identical trial;
  - checks the case and punctuation rules for these.
- **Model reading:**
  - an observation whose quotes don't match is dropped;
  - more than two observations are cut to two;
  - with no provider, only the code layer shows and nothing reports itself as broken.
- **Tracker:**
  - a multi-sentence selection is kept as the original;
  - a stale source blocks apply and keeps the trial;
  - apply is one undo step;
  - grammar findings don't block apply.
- **One e2e test:** select, edit, see the gone list, toggle Original/Trial, apply, then Undo restores the original.

## Acceptance criteria

1. A cold-start open shows the paragraph, the original and the trial with no network and no ledger history.
2. No generated wording appears anywhere on the surface.
3. Every model observation quotes text that exists, and it adds to the code layer without replacing it.
4. Keyboard path works: Mod+Enter uses the revision, Esc keeps the original.

## Unresolved objections

- **The "obvious edit" objection is not answered.** The writer did delete "probably". Whether naming it changes any decisions is an empirical question I cannot settle. Kill criterion: if, over a week of the user's own revisions, the gone list or the reading never leads them to restore or reconsider anything, retire the bench and leave ordinary editing plus Undo.
- **The code layer misses meaning changes that remove no words**, such as swapping "allowed" for "forced" or reordering emphasis. Catching those depends on the model reading, which can be wrong or invent distinctions.
- **Running the model reading automatically costs hosted credit.** Gating it on the code layer's flags limits the cost, but also stops it from catching unflagged changes.
- **This does nothing for a writer who is stuck with no idea.** Wordcraft-style users lose generation entirely.
- **Removing Words, Place and Alternatives deletes documented, shipped behaviour.** The parent should decide whether to delete or hide them.
- **Park and persisted version history** are still the more valuable longer-term additions. Both are deferred for coordination and data-location reasons, not because they were rejected.

# Plan Execution Graph

Turn a decision-complete plan into an executable directed acyclic graph (DAG), then coordinate bounded subagents without duplicated work or file conflicts.

## Workflow

### 1. Ground the graph

Before delegating:

- Read repository instructions and relevant skills.
- Inspect `git status` and treat pre-existing edits as protected.
- Identify required generated files, migrations, quality gates, and runtime verification.
- Separate discoverable repository facts from user decisions fixed by the plan.
- Do not delegate the immediate blocking step when the coordinator can execute it faster locally.

### 2. Decompose by deliverable

Create nodes that produce concrete artifacts, not vague research activity. Prefer:

- A short preflight or audit node.
- Foundation nodes for shared types, contracts, schemas, or primitives.
- Parallel implementation nodes with disjoint write sets.
- A coordinator-only integration node for protected or highly coupled files.
- Test and runtime-verification nodes after integration.

Each node must specify:

- Stable ID and concise name.
- Agent role: explorer, worker, verifier, or coordinator.
- Exact responsibility and output.
- Owned files or subsystem.
- Dependencies.
- Acceptance gate.
- Explicit exclusions when nearby work belongs to another node.

### 3. Build dependency edges

Add an edge only when a downstream task consumes an upstream artifact or decision.

Use these dependency rules:

- Shared contracts precede all consumers.
- Backend and client adapters precede feature integration when their interfaces change.
- UI primitives precede surfaces that render them.
- Generated API or codegen follows source changes but precedes typecheck.
- Tests depend on the interfaces or behavior they validate.
- Integration precedes broad verification.
- Runtime verification follows a successful production build.

Avoid false serialization. Independent file sets should run in the same wave.

### 4. Assign safe ownership

For every coding worker:

- Give an exclusive, disjoint write set.
- State that the worker is not alone in the codebase.
- Instruct it not to revert others' edits.

## Register

product

## Users

Writers, editors, researchers, and technically comfortable creators who want a focused drafting room with structured editorial feedback. They are usually trying to move from a vague brief or partial draft into a clearer manuscript, then export or publish it.

## Product Purpose

Twyne is a local-first writing desk with an AI-assisted room of editors. It helps writers define a project dossier, draft in rich text, receive persona feedback, score work against a rubric, manage citations, sync across devices when signed in, and publish or export finished work. Success means the writer keeps ownership and momentum while the product makes revision concrete.

## Brand Personality

Editorial, exacting, literary. The product should feel like a working writer's room rather than generic SaaS: opinionated, calm, and serious about craft without getting precious.

## Anti-references

Do not make Twyne look like a generic AI chat app, a growth dashboard, a blank note-taking clone, or a loud marketing funnel. Avoid decorative UI that competes with the manuscript, vague AI productivity claims, and controls that obscure where drafts and keys are stored.

## Design Principles

- Keep the manuscript central.
- Make data movement explicit: local, synced, published, or sent to a provider.
- Use standard controls for standard tasks, dressed in Twyne's editorial system.
- Prefer concise copy that names the actual action.
- Preserve writer trust through clear export, privacy, and account controls.

## Accessibility & Inclusion

Aim for WCAG AA contrast and keyboard-operable controls. Important interactions should work with semantic HTML where possible. Respect reduced-motion preferences, avoid color-only state, and keep long-form reading comfortable on mobile and desktop.

# From cards to instruments

Design proposal and implementation record, 2026-10-09. Responds to `audit.md` (2026-10-05) and its proposed cards.

## Implementation status

The first instrument slices now exist in the working tree: complete sentence comparisons and word choices, nearby placement, contextual narration, manuscript Threads, entity presence and bounded readings, paragraph readings and Charter exceptions, explicit local model packs, a durable Task desk, and a Scene bench with source inventory and separate writer ideas. This is an implementation map, not a deployment or live-provider certification. The original proposal below remains intact as a design target; its future capabilities are not promises about the current interface. In particular, automatic semantic placement ranking, generated bridges and merges, cross-folio scene continuity, cast voices, tension-curve soundtracks, and image/video generation are not supplied by this implementation.

## The reframe: three places help can live

Replace "cards" with **instruments**: tools that point at a span and change it, always with a preview and undo.

1. **In the line.** Underlines, ghost text, and small glyphs placed directly in the manuscript, like Grammarly but for a literary writer. Examples: grammar (Harper, already shipped), word alternatives, words a model finds unlikely in context, repetition. All of these run locally.
2. **Between lines (threads).** Typed links between spans: _repeats, sets up, pays off, supports, contradicts, answers, refers back to_. They appear when the writer selects or hovers with a modifier key, or when a "Threads" lens is turned on. The curve-drawing code in `flow-surface.tsx` already draws card-to-passage links; extend it to draw sentence-to-sentence links with labels.
3. **On the bench.** A focused workbench opened on one span: the Sentence bench, the Paragraph bench, and the Scene bench (described below).

**Surfacing rule.** Nothing appears automatically unless it carries a change ready to apply or opens a working instrument with one click. Pure information ("You wrote this earlier") is not allowed. The current echo card either becomes **Recover**, which offers a concrete merge, or a **thread**, which names the relationship.

## Instrument 1: the Sentence bench (replaces Sentence Lab)

Fix the data first:

- **Settled attempts only.** Record a wording only when the sentence is complete (ends in terminal punctuation), the cursor has left it or about 5 s have passed, Harper reports no spelling error touching the edited span (this catches `carr`), and it is not a prefix of a later wording. Collapse near-duplicates (fewer than 3 characters different).
- **A sentence ledger.** Give each sentence a stable ID that is mapped through transactions. Re-match by fuzzy similarity rather than index, so split, join, cut, and paste preserve history. Detect moves: text deleted and reinserted at least 90% similar, either in one transaction or by cut and then paste. Each entry keeps `wordings[]` and `placements[]`.

The bench has five sections. Every candidate is a complete sentence shown as a word-level diff against the current one. Hovering a candidate previews it as ghost text in place, between the real neighbouring sentences.

1. **Rewrite.** Three to five complete alternatives. Each shows facts computed in code (`−6 words`, `active`, `no hedge`) and verified tags (`keeps meaning 0.94`, `fits your register`), plus a provenance chip: _yours (4 min ago)_, _rule_, _on-device_, _Claude_, _spoken_. Offline sources are the best settled attempt plus rule transforms (front a trailing clause, cut intensifiers and hedges, turn a nominalisation back into a verb, split at a semicolon or conjunction, join with the next sentence), each checked by Harper. On desktop, MiniCPM fills in automatically.
2. **Words.** Click any word to see alternatives in context. Thesaurus candidates are ranked by the masked model's probability in the actual sentence. Jev adds nuance (`stronger`, `plainer`, `more formal`) and a `changes meaning` warning. Repeated words in the paragraph are underlined.
3. **Place.** Insertion carets in the manuscript mark the strongest slots, each with a reason. Some reasons are deterministic: a sentence starting with _This_, _These_, _It_, or _Such_ needs its antecedent before it. Others come from embedding coherence with the neighbours on each side, or from a Jev Choice over slot IDs. Uses `placements[]`: "You've tried this in 3 places; read each one in context." One click moves it, with undo.
4. **Hear.** Supertonic reads the previous sentence followed by each candidate, entirely offline. Rhythm problems are easier to hear than to see.
5. **Say it.** The writer records themselves explaining what the sentence should say. Whisper transcribes it; rules or a model tidy it; the result becomes a candidate. This replaces the "Say it plainly first" template with an actual action.

The bench opens from a struggle signal (three _settled_ rewrites), after a sentence has moved twice (opens on Place), or on request from the selection menu or a shortcut.

| Description             | See it, What's missing, Hear it                             |
| Dialogue                | Cast voices, Does each speaker sound distinct?              |
| Two ranges (Alt+select) | Name the relation, Bridge, Merge, Which is stronger, Swap   |

## Instrument 3: Threads

- Number the sentences of the current section (`S001`…). Jev Choice accepts at most 255 options, and state plus the longest question must fit in 32k tokens, so use section windows plus a second pass (the cookbook's two-pass approach).
- Local embeddings propose candidate pairs at no cost. One Jev request labels them: a Choice among _repeats / supports / contradicts / sets up / pays off / answers / no real relation_, plus a Noul for whether the link exists (Choice probabilities always sum to 1).
- Proactive threads that come with an action: a **setup with no payoff** ("'the ledger' is introduced in ¶2 and never comes back": choose a later sentence or add one); **two sentences doing the same job** (offer Merge with an actual merged sentence, or keep the stronger, chosen by Jev); a **dangling reference** (_this_ with nothing before it to refer to: offer Move).
- Replace the 14-word regex anchors with ProseMirror decorations keyed to ledger IDs.

## Instrument 4: the Scene bench (where media models earn their place)

Images, music, and video help a writer only if they show the gap between what is on the page and what the writer imagines.

- **See it.** Jev runs a Noul for each scene dimension (place, time of day, light, weather, who is present, what they wear, spatial layout, sound, smell). The image prompt is built **only from spans of the writer's text**, which Jev selects rather than writes. The result is the image plus a list of **what it had to invent**. Each invented item links to the spot where the writer could specify it. That list is the useful output; the image is the hook.
- **Continuity** without images: extract attributes as text ("Mara's coat: red, ch. 2"; "blue, ch. 7") and flag contradictions as threads across folios.
- **Voices.** Assign TTS voices to speakers and play the dialogue back. If two characters sound the same aloud, they also read the same.
- **Tension curve.** Jev Scores per paragraph (tension, pace, warmth) plotted across a chapter cost almost nothing and show pacing. An optional generated music cue turns the curve into sound, a quick way to check whether a scene feels as tense as intended.
- **Blocking.** Positions and movements chosen from spans become a simple top-down SVG. Generated video ("animate the beat") stays a late opt-in for screenwriters; the diagram does more for the writing at a tiny fraction of the cost.

## Local language models as grammar and style checks

- **Surprise underline.** A masked model scores each word in context. Unlikely words catch real-word errors that Harper misses (_form/from_, wrong prepositions, malapropisms), and the model's top replacements become suggestions.
- **Redundancy.** Neighbouring sentences with very similar embeddings.
- **Cohesion gaps.** Similarity between neighbours falls below this draft's own baseline; this is the trigger for Bridge.
- **Voice match.** Distance from the centroid of the writer's voice samples in the notebook. Phrase it as an observation, never a verdict.
- **Clichés.** Phrase embeddings compared against a small bundled list.
- **Drift from the dossier.** Similarity to the stated goal, continuous across the draft, with Jev confirming only at the peaks.

| What does S depend on?          | Choice + Noul exists                                                 | Section with IDs                              | sentence IDs                 |

Sentence work is one level of six. Help needs to reach every level, and the most useful findings often span the whole document. Examples: an essay that slides between "I" and an editorial "we", a character called Hollins in chapter 2 and Hollis in chapter 9, a section that disappears from the argument.

| Level           | Examples of what to notice                                    | Who finds it                   |

| Word            | Repeated words, near-synonyms, unlikely words                 | Code, fill-mask model          |
| Sentence        | Rewording, placement, rhythm                                  | Sentence bench (above)         |
| Paragraph       | Missing support, cohesion, how much it carries                | Jev passage scores, embeddings |
| Section / scene | Balance, order, tension, point of view                        | Jev, outline, embeddings       |
| Piece           | Stance, tense, naming, terminology, promises, arcs, the score | Ledgers (below)                |
| Collection      | Story bible, repeated anecdotes, voice over time              | Cross-folio index              |

content.text:
Compare a revision is implemented and working. Unit, e2e and in-browser checks pass, but nothing has been tested against a real model. The browser runs of "Read the difference" used a mock provider, so they show the app handles a reading correctly, not that a real model's readings are any good. It is also still a hypothesis that this bench is worth opening; that needs real use to settle. Nothing is committed or deployed.

**What changed**
- **Entry:** the selection button is now "Compare a revision" (the card title too). It finds the sentence by where the selection or cursor is, so it picks the right copy when the same sentence appears twice. It refuses, with a reason, a selection covering several sentences, one crossing paragraphs, or a passage it can't locate exactly once. It never opens by itself: repeated rewriting only leaves the margin tick, and the open-after-three-moves path is gone.
- **The bench:** the original stays fixed, with one editable copy below it. The paragraph is shown by default with a word diff, and you can switch between Changes, Revision and Original. Also there: Use revision, Keep original, Copy revision, Preview in manuscript, Hear it in context, and the existing Ask an editor link. Fragments and several sentences are allowed, and grammar never blocks your own wording; the only limits are length (1,200 characters) and no line breaks.
- **Use revision:** one undo step, and the caret goes back to the end of the revised sentence. It only replaces the words that changed, so bold, italics, links and notes elsewhere in the sentence are kept. If a change would cut through a note or mix formatting, it refuses with an explanation rather than flattening anything. If the sentence or its paragraph changes while the bench is open, applying is blocked and your revision stays there to copy. Escape or Keep original closes without touching the page.
- **Read the difference:** only when you click it, through the prose provider configured in Settings, one request per click. It returns at most two observations, each quoting the original, the revision and any paragraph text it relies on. Those quotes are checked in code, and any that don't match are dropped and counted.
  - Editing the revision, or any change to the sentence or paragraph, discards the reading. A late answer for older text is thrown away, and Stop cancels.
  - An empty result says only "The model returned no observations for this revision."
  - There is no fallback to Jev or a small on-device model, no rewriting and no ranking.
- **Removed:** the Rewrite/Words/Place/Hear tabs, generated and regex rewrites, the thesaurus, placement, the Compare panel, meaning probabilities, the per-row caveats and the automatic opening. I deleted their helper code only after checking the Sentence bench was its only user.

**Files**
- Bench: `sentence-bench.tsx` and `.css`, `catalog.ts`, fixtures, stories.
- Logic: `src/utils/sentence-bench.ts`, `src/utils/in-flow-tools.ts`, the Sentence Lab parts of `struggle-tracker.ts`, and the "Compare a revision" label in `struggle-signals.ts`.
- Entry points: `selection-actions.tsx` and `local-writing-tools.tsx`. An edited transcript now becomes the revision instead of a candidate.
- Tests: `sentence-bench.test.ts`, `in-flow-tools.test.ts`, `catalog.test.ts` and `struggle-tracker.test.ts`; in `e2e/`, `instruments.e2e.ts`, `instrument-room.e2e.ts` and `fixtures/instrument-room.ts`, plus the two Sentence bench visual baselines.
- Docs: `docs/writing-instruments.md`, the manual page (`src/routes/docs/index.tsx`), the guide, the film transcript, and the narration script with its audio re-rendered.
- `src/global.css`, which already had other people's changes: I added one block so the selection toolbar wraps at 390 px. The longer label had been pushing "More" off-screen.
- I did not touch `twyne-editor.tsx`, `flow-surface.tsx`, `comment-mark.ts`, the persona files, Convex, or any of the other changes already in the working tree.

**Checks**
- Unit tests: 98 pass across the eight affected files. Typecheck: zero errors. ESLint is clean on the changed source; the e2e files aren't in the lint project, as before. Client build passes.
- E2E: all 16 tests in `instruments.e2e.ts` and `instrument-room.e2e.ts` pass under the visual config. One earlier failure was a test still expecting the old room question; I updated it.
- Real browser (headless Chromium against the running dev server), at 1440 and 390 px with a long paragraph:
  - Opening makes no bench request and changes nothing.
  - The second copy of a duplicated sentence is targeted correctly.
  - A late reading for an edited revision is discarded.
  - One grounded observation is shown, and the invented quote is dropped and counted.
  - Ctrl/Cmd+Enter applies to the right copy only, focus returns to the manuscript, and one Undo restores it.
  - No page errors.
- With a provider configured, the existing research-librarian feature made a request right after load, before the bench opened. That is separate from this work.

**Server:** http://127.0.0.1:5174/editor/ is the dev server already running from this checkout. I opened it in the T3 preview, but that profile has no folio and redirects to dossier creation. I didn't write test data into that profile.

**Remaining risks**
- Hosted users: "Read the difference" only uses a provider the user configured in Settings. Hosted accounts without one get "needs a prose model connected", because there is no hosted route for this tool and adding one would mean a Convex change.
- Whether readings are useful, and whether this beats editing plus Undo or the existing Ask an editor, is unproven. If readings turn out to be obvious or empty in real use, retiring the bench is the honest outcome.
- The "Words in context" on-device pack can still be downloaded, but nothing uses it now. Removing it or its copy is your call.
- The recorded film and the first Ask-the-room screenshot still show the old bench. I labelled both as such rather than re-recording them.
- On desktop, a sentence low on the page can put Use revision below the fold, because the margin card sits beside its sentence. This was already the case before.
- When "Read the difference" is cancelled or replaced, the provider request isn't aborted, because the transport has no abort hook; its answer is simply discarded.
